subject: Pathology
summary: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is a subtype of AML driven by t(15;17) that presents with DIC and responds dramatically to ATRA/ATO. Early recognition and prompt differentiation therapy saves lives.

sections.p: APL is defined by the presence of t(15;17) PML‑RARA fusion, hypergranular promyelocytes with Auer rods, and a high risk of DIC. Diagnosis requires morphology, cytogenetics or FISH, and coagulation profile.
b: Hypergranular promyelocytes + Auer rods are classic

t.b: If absent, consider other AML subtypes
If unavailable, use RT‑PCR for PML‑RARA
Low fibrinogen and high D‑dimer indicate active DIC

sections.p: APL is staged by the WHO AML system; risk is stratified by leukocyte count and platelet level. High‑risk disease has WBC >10,000/µL or platelets <40,000/µL.
The primary cause is the chromosomal translocation t(15;17). Secondary factors include infections (HIV, TB), malaria, and herbal remedies that may delay diagnosis.
b: t(15;17) PML‑RARA fusion is the driver
Infections can mask symptoms and delay care

sections.p: Patients often present with fatigue, bruising, petechiae, and bleeding due to DIC. Fever and infections are common secondary features.
b: Easy bruising and petechiae from DIC

sections.p: Key tests include CBC, peripheral smear, coagulation profile, cytogenetics/FISH, and bone marrow aspirate. In low‑resource settings, a smear and coagulation panel are critical.
Rapidly progressive DIC, intracranial hemorrhage, and early relapse are life‑threatening. Monitor for differentiation syndrome and organ dysfunction.
b: Severe bleeding or sudden drop in platelets

sections.p: Immediate initiation of ATRA plus arsenic trioxide (ATO) induces differentiation and controls DIC. Supportive care includes transfusions and antifibrinolytics. Avoid cytotoxic chemotherapy until differentiation is achieved.
Regular CBCs and coagulation studies monitor remission. Long‑term surveillance for relapse is essential. Prevention focuses on early recognition and treatment of infections.
Other AML subtypes (e.g., AML‑M2), myelodysplastic syndromes, and severe infections can mimic APL.
Coagulation tests may be falsely normal early in DIC; peripheral smear may miss rare promyelocytes. Cytogenetics may be delayed in low‑resource settings.
b: Early DIC can have normal fibrinogen

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe bleeding, loss of consciousness, or rapid drop in platelet count

faq.q: What is the most urgent treatment for APL?
faq.a: Start ATRA and arsenic trioxide immediately to stop DIC and induce remission.
Yes, with early differentiation therapy most patients achieve long‑term remission.

faq.q: Why is DIC common in APL?
faq.a: Promyelocytes release procoagulant granules that trigger widespread clotting and consumption of clotting factors.

exam: Explain how t(15;17) leads to DIC and why ATRA/ATO are effective.
Describe the laboratory work‑up for a patient with suspected APL and interpret key results.
Outline the management steps for a patient presenting with severe bleeding due to APL.
